questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Work Done by a Force
questions.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $3.5\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis with an acceleration of magnitude $2{x}^{3}\,{m/s}^{2}$ acting in the direction $OP.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=0$ to $x=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
The work done by a force $F=F(x)$ in moving a particle from $x={x}_{1}$ to $x={x}_{2}$ is given by

$$
W={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($J$).

Using Newton's second law of motion, the force required to accelerate a particle of mass $3.5\,kg$ at a rate of $2{x}^{3}\,{m/s}^{2}$ is

$$
F=ma=3.5\cdot 2{x}^{3}=7{x}^{3}\,N.
$$

Now, substituting the known values into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{0}^{2}7{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{7}{4}{x}^{4}\,{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{7}{4}(16-0) \\  & =28\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($J$).

questions.worked_solution:
The work done by a force $F=F(x)$ in moving a particle from $x={x}_{1}$ to $x={x}_{2}$ is given by

$$
W={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($J$).

Using Newton's second law of motion, the force required to accelerate a particle of mass $2.5\,kg$ at a rate of $(4-{x}^{2})\,{m/s}^{2}$ is

$$
F=ma=2.5\cdot (4-{x}^{2})=(10-2.5{x}^{2})\,N.
$$

Now, substituting the known values into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(10-2.5{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[10x-\frac{5}{6}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(10(1)-\frac{5}{6}({1}^{3}))-(10(0)-\frac{5}{6}({0}^{3})) \\  & =10-\frac{5}{6} \\  & =\frac{55}{6}\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $4\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis with an acceleration of magnitude $(\frac{1}{x}+{x}^{3})\,{m/s}^{2}$ acting in the direction $OP.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=e.$
questions.worked_solution:
The work done by a force $F=F(x)$ in moving a particle from $x={x}_{1}$ to $x={x}_{2}$ is given by

$$
W={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($J$).

Using Newton's second law of motion, the force required to accelerate a particle of mass $4\,kg$ at a rate of $(\frac{1}{x}+{x}^{3})\,{m/s}^{2}$ is

$$
F=ma=4(\frac{1}{x}+{x}^{3})=(\frac{4}{x}+4{x}^{3})\,N.
$$

Now, substituting the known values into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{1}^{e}(\frac{4}{x}+4{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[4\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+{x}^{4}]}_{1}^{e} \\  & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡e+{e}^{4}-(4\operatorname{ln}⁡1+{1}^{4}) \\  & =4+{e}^{4}-0-1 \\  & =({e}^{4}+3)\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Kinetic Energy of a Particle
questions.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $\frac{8}{5}\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude $3t\,{m/s}^{2},$ where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing $x,$ and $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the change in kinetic energy of the particle between the times $t=1\,s$ and $t=2\,s.$
questions.worked_solution:
The change in kinetic energy of a particle with mass $m,$ initial velocity ${v}_{0},$ and final velocity ${v}_{1}$ is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($J$).

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int 3t\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0=\frac{3}{2}({0}^{2})+C\,⟹\,C=0.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}.$ In particular, its inital velocity at time $t=1\,s$ and final velocity at time $t=2\,s$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{0} & =v(1)=\frac{3}{2}({1}^{2})=\frac{3}{2}\,m/s, \\ {v}_{1} & =v(2)=\frac{3}{2}({2}^{2})=6\,m/s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change in kinetic energy of the particle between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ\,\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{8}{5}\cdot {6}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{8}{5}\cdot {(\frac{3}{2})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{144}{5}-\frac{9}{5} \\  & =27\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

The change in kinetic energy of a particle with mass $m,$ initial velocity ${v}_{0},$ and final velocity ${v}_{1}$ is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($J$).

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int 2{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =-2{e}^{-t}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0=-2{e}^{-0}+C\,⟹\,C=2.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=2-2{e}^{-t}.$ In particular, its inital velocity at time $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,s$ and final velocity at time $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡4\,s$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{0} & =v(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)=2-2{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}=1\,m/s, \\ {v}_{1} & =v(\operatorname{ln}⁡4)=2-2{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡4}=\frac{3}{2}\,m/s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change in kinetic energy of the particle between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ\,\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot {(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot {(1)}^{2} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}-1 \\  & =\frac{5}{4}\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $6\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude $(1+{t}^{2})\,{m/s}^{2},$ where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing $x,$ and $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the particle's kinetic energy at time $t=1\,s.$
questions.worked_solution:
The kinetic energy of a particle with mass $m$ and velocity $v$ is given by

$$
\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2}.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($J$).

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int (1+{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =t+\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0=0+\frac{1}{3}({0}^{3})+C\,⟹\,C=0.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=t+\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}.$ In particular, its velocity at time $t=1\,s$ is

$$
v=v(1)=1+\frac{1}{3}({1}^{3})=\frac{4}{3}\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, the kinetic energy of the particle at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 6\cdot {(\frac{4}{3})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 6\cdot \frac{16}{9} \\  & =\frac{16}{3}\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Work-Energy Principle To Find the Work Done by a Force
questions.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $2\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a resultant force. The particle's velocity is $2t\,m/s,$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the work done by the force between the times $t=1\,s$ and $t=2\,s.$
questions.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

The particle's velocity is given by $v(t)=2t,$ where $t$ is time in seconds. So, the particle's initial velocity, at $t=1$, is

$$
{v}_{0}=v(1)=2(1)=2\,m/s,
$$

and final velocity, at $t=2$, is

$$
{v}_{1}=v(2)=2(2)=4\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =Δ\,\text{KE} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot (4)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot (2)^{2} \\  & =16-4 \\  & =12\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $2\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a resultant force. The particle's acceleration is $(3{t}^{2}+4)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=1\,m/s$ when $t=0\,s,$ calculate the work done by the force between the times $t=1\,s$ and $t=2\,s.$
questions.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

The acceleration of the particle is given by $a(t)=3{t}^{2}+4,$ where $t$ is time in seconds.
We find the velocity $v(t)$ of the particle by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (3{t}^{2}+4)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{3}+4t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
1=(0)^{3}+4(0)+C\,⟹\,C=1.
$$

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)={t}^{3}+4t+1.$
In particular, the particle's initial velocity, at $t=1,$ is

$$
{v}_{0}=v(1)=(1)^{3}+4(1)+1=6\,m/s,
$$

and final velocity, at $t=2,$ is

$$
{v}_{1}=v(2)=(2)^{3}+4(2)+1=17\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =Δ\,\text{KE} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot {17}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot {6}^{2} \\  & =289-36 \\  & =253\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

The acceleration of the particle is given by $a(t)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}+1,$ where $t$ is time in seconds.
We find the velocity $v(t)$ of the particle by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{t}+t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
2=\sqrt{0}+0+C\,⟹\,C=2.
$$

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\sqrt{t}+t+2.$
In particular, the particle's initial velocity, at $t=1,$ is

$$
{v}_{0}=v(1)=\sqrt{1}+1+2=4\,m/s,
$$

and final velocity, at $t=4$, is

$$
{v}_{1}=v(4)=\sqrt{4}+4+2=8\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =Δ\,\text{KE} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 6\cdot {8}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 6\cdot {4}^{2} \\  & =192-48 \\  & =144\,J.\end{aligned}

$$

and final velocity, at $t=2,$ is

$$
{v}_{1}=v(2)={2}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{9}{2}\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =Δ\,\text{KE} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 8\cdot {(\frac{9}{2})}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 8\cdot {2}^{2} \\  & =81-16 \\  & =65\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $4\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of the force of magnitude $({x}^{3}-4)\,N$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, the particle was initially at $x=3$, and the particle has velocity $v=10\,m/s$ at $x=5,$ calculate the particle's initial velocity.
questions.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=3$ to $x=5:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{3}^{5}({x}^{3}-4)\,\text{d}x \\  & =(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}-4x){|}_{3}^{5} \\  & =(\frac{625}{4}-20)-(\frac{81}{4}-12) \\  & =128\,J\end{aligned}
$$

The particle has velocity $v=10\,m/s$ at $x=5.$ So, we can find the velocity ${v}_{0}$ at $x=3$ using the work-energy principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =\frac{1}{2}{m}_{1}{v}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\ 128 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {10}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {v}_{0}^{2} \\ 128 & =200-2{v}_{0}^{2} \\ 2{v}_{0}^{2} & =72 \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =36 \\ {v}_{0} & =\pm 6.\end{aligned}
$$

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration. 

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at $x=3$ is $6\,m/s.$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $1\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of the force of magnitude $(3{x}^{2}+2)\,N$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that distances along the $x$-axis are measured in meters, the particle is initially at the origin, and the particle has velocity $v=7\,m/s$ at $x=2,$ find the particle's change in velocity in moving from $x=0$ to $x=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=0$ to $x=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(3{x}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[{x}^{3}+2x]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =8+4-0 \\  & =12\,J\end{aligned}
$$

The particle has velocity $v=7\,m/s$ at $x=2.$ So, we can find the velocity ${v}_{0}$ at $x=0$ using the work-energy principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\ 12 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot {7}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot {v}_{0}^{2} \\ 12 & =\frac{49}{2}-\frac{1}{2}{v}_{0}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}{v}_{0}^{2} & =\frac{25}{2} \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =25 \\ {v}_{0} & =\pm 5.\end{aligned}
$$

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration. 

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at $x=0$ is $5\,m/s.$

Finally, the particle's change in velocity from $x=0$ to $x=2$ is

$$
{v}_{1}-{v}_{0}=7-5=2\,m/s.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(8-x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[8x-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =(24-\frac{9}{2})-(8-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =12\,J\end{aligned}
$$

The particle has velocity $v=6\,m/s$ at $x=1.$ So, we can find the velocity ${v}_{1}$ at $x=3$ using the work-energy principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\ 12 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 6\cdot {v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 6\cdot {6}^{2} \\ 12 & =3{v}_{1}^{2}-108 \\ 3{v}_{1} & =120 \\ {v}_{1}^{2} & =40 \\ {v}_{1} & =\pm \sqrt{40} \\ {v}_{1} & =\pm 2\sqrt{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration. 

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at $x=3$ is $2\sqrt{10}\,m/s.$

questions.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}+x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-\frac{2}{x}){|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =(8-\frac{1}{2})-(\frac{1}{2}-2) \\  & =9\,J\end{aligned}
$$

The particle has velocity $v=3\,m/s$ at $x=4.$ So, we can find the velocity ${v}_{0}$ at $x=1$ using the work-energy principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =\frac{1}{2}{m}_{1}{v}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\ 9 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot {3}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot {v}_{0}^{2} \\ 9 & =\frac{27}{2}-\frac{3}{2}{v}_{0}^{2} \\ \frac{3}{2}{v}_{0}^{2} & =\frac{9}{2} \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =3 \\ {v}_{0} & =\pm \sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration. 

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at $x=1$ is $\sqrt{3}\,m/s.$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $7\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of the force of magnitude $(2x+3)\,N$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, the particle was initially at $x=1,$ and the particle has velocity $v=2\sqrt{5}\,m/s$ at $x=3,$ calculate the particle's initial velocity.
questions.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(2x+3)\,\text{d}x \\  & =({x}^{2}+3x){|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =(9+9)-(1+3) \\  & =14\,J\end{aligned}
$$

The particle has velocity $v=2\sqrt{5}\,m/s$ at $x=3.$ So, we can find the velocity ${v}_{0}$ at $x=1$ using the work-energy principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =\frac{1}{2}{m}_{1}{v}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\ 14 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 7\cdot (2\sqrt{5})^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 7\cdot {v}_{0}^{2} \\ 14 & =70-\frac{7}{2}{v}_{0}^{2} \\ \frac{7}{2}{v}_{0}^{2} & =56 \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =16 \\ {v}_{0} & =\pm 4.\end{aligned}
$$

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration. 

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at $x=1$ is $4\,m/s.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Work Done by a Force
canonical_examples.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $3\,\rm{kg}$ moves along the $x$-axis with an acceleration of magnitude $(1 + 2x^2)\,\rm{m/s}^2$ acting in the direction $OP.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=0$ to $x=2.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The work done by a force $F=F(x)$ in moving a particle from $x=x_1$ to $x=x_2$ is given by

$$
W = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} F(x) \,\textrm{d}x.
$$

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($\rm{J}$).

Using Newton's second law of motion, the force required to accelerate a particle of mass $3\,\rm{kg}$ at a rate of $(1 + 2x^2)\,\rm{m/s}^2$ is

$$
F = ma = 3 \cdot (1 + 2x^2) = (3 + 6x^2) \,\rm{N}.
$$

Now, substituting the known values into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(3+6{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[3x+2{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =3(2)+2({2}^{3})-(3(0)+2({0}^{3})) \\  & =6+16-0 \\  & =22\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Kinetic Energy of a Particle
canonical_examples.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $2\,\rm{kg}$ moves along the $x$-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude $(4t+1)\,\rm{m/s}^2,$ where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing $x,$ and $t \geq 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the change in kinetic energy of the particle between the times $t = 1\,\rm{s}$ and $t = 2\,\rm{s}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The change in kinetic energy of a particle with mass $m,$ initial velocity $v_0,$ and final velocity $v_1$ is given by

$$
\Delta \, \text{KE} = \dfrac{1}{2}mv_{1}^{2} - \dfrac{1}{2}mv_{0}^{2}.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($\rm{J}$).

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int (4t+1)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =2{t}^{2}+t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0) = 0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0 = 2(0^2) + 0 + C
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
C = 0.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t) = 2t^2 + t.$ In particular, its inital velocity at time $t = 1\,\rm{s}$ and final velocity at time $t = 2\,\rm{s}$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{0} & =v(1)=2({1}^{2})+1=3\,m/s, \\ {v}_{1} & =v(2)=2({2}^{2})+2=10\,m/s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change in kinetic energy of the particle between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ\,\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot {10}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot {3}^{2} \\  & =100-9 \\  & =91\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Applying the Work-Energy Principle To Find the Work Done by a Force
canonical_examples.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $1\,\rm{kg}$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a resultant force. The displacement of the particle is given by $(t^2-2t+3)\,\rm{m},$ where $t \geq 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the work done by the force between the times $t=1\,\rm{s}$ and $t=3\,\rm{s}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W
= 
\Delta\, \text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
\Delta\, \text{KE} = \dfrac12 m v_1^2 - \dfrac12 m v_0^2
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, $v_0$ is its initial velocity, and $v_1$ is its final velocity.

The displacement of the particle is given by $x(t)=t^2-2t+3,$ where $t$ is time in seconds.
We find the velocity $v(t)$ of the particle by differentiating the displacement with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-2t+3) \\  & =2t-2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the particle's initial velocity, at $t=1$, is

$$
v_0 = v(1) =  2(1) -2 = 0\,\rm{m/s},
$$

and its final velocity, at $t=3$, is

$$
v_1 = v(3) = 2(3) -2= 4\,\rm{m/s}.
$$

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =Δ\,\text{KE} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot (4)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot {0}^{2} \\  & =8-0 \\  & =8\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $2\,\rm{kg}$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a force of magnitude $(x+3)\,\rm{N}$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, and the particle has velocity $v=2\,\rm{m/s}$ at $x=2,$ calculate the velocity of the particle at $x=4.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W
= 
\Delta\, \text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
\Delta\, \text{KE} = \dfrac12 m v_1^2 - \dfrac12 m v_0^2
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, $v_0$ is its initial velocity, and $v_1$ is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=2$ to $x=4{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{4}(x+3)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+3x]}_{2}^{4} \\  & =(8+12)-(2+6) \\  & =12\,J\end{aligned}
$$

The particle has velocity $v=2\,\rm{m/s}$ at $x=2.$ So, we can find the velocity $v_1$ at $x=4$ using the work-energy principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\ 12 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot {v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot {2}^{2} \\ 12 & ={v}_{1}^{2}-4 \\ {v}_{1}^{2} & =16 \\ {v}_{1} & =\pm 4.\end{aligned}
$$

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration. 

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at $x=4$ is $4\,\rm{m/s}.$
